Bone Healing
The two basic mechanisms of bone healing are direct intramembranous bone formation
and endochondral bone formation. Direct intramembranous bone formation occurs
when pluripotent stem cells differentiate into cells of the osteoblast lineage and secrete
unmineralized osteoid matrix, which subsequently mineralizes to form mature bone

tissue without passing through a cartilage phase. Endochondral bone formation is more
reminiscent of embryologic bone formation, in which a cartilaginous anlage undergoes
progression to hypertrophic chondrocytes, followed by vascular invasion and then
conversion of the cartilage matrix to ossified bone, which later remodels according to
Wolff’s law (form follows function) based on the stress and strain experienced by the
newly formed bone (Resource 1).
Osteoblasts are derived from mesenchymal stem cells, which can be mobilized from the
bone marrow or locally from the perivascular cell space. They are responsible for bone
matrix synthesis and its subsequent mineralization.
Osteocytes are osteoblasts that ultimately become incorporated within the newly
formed unmineralized osteoid matrix that eventually becomes calcified bone.
Osteocytes are thought to play a regulatory role in mature bone via an extensive
network of cell processes that extend through canaliculi and can respond to changes in
physical forces on bone and subsequently communicate with cells on the bone surface
about increasing formation or resorption.
Osteoclasts are large multinucleated cells, similar to macrophages, derived from the
hematopoietic lineage. Osteoclasts facilitate resorption of mineralized tissue and attach
to the bone surface at sites of active bone resorption. Their characteristic feature is a
ruffled edge at which active resorption takes place because of the secretion of
hydrochloric acid and bone-resorbing enzymes, which digest bone matrix. A
communication system between osteoblasts and osteoclasts results in coupling of bone
turnover.
Chondroblasts and chondrocytes are two types of cells found in cartilage during
endochondral bone formation. Chondroblasts are immature cells that secrete the
extracellular matrix of the cartilage, whereas chondrocytes are involved in the
maintenance of cartilage. After the chondroblasts are surrounded by extracellular
matrix, they become chondrocytes. The phenotype of chondrocytes may vary depending
on whether they are articular or deep in the cartilage tissue. During endochondral
ossification, chondrocytes hypertrophy and secrete specific signals that initiate vascular
invasion and conversion to mineralized bone matrix.

Fibroblasts are the principal active cells of connective tissue. They are large, flat,
elongated (spindle-shaped) cells with processes extending from the ends of the cell
body. The cell nucleus is flat and oval. Fibroblasts produce tropocollagen, which is the
forerunner of collagen, and ground substance, an amorphous gel-like matrix that fills the
spaces between cells in connective tissue. Fibroblasts can form fibrous tissue that can
interrupt bone formation in a fracture callus or bone graft incorporation situation.
Excessive motion of a bone healing construct may result in fibrous tissue rather than
cartilage (endochondral healing) in a slightly flexible construct or bone (direct primary
bone healing) in a rigid construct.
Primary bone healing occurs with rigid bone fixation constructs that provide absolute
stability. If open reduction and internal fixation is performed, the initial fracture
hematoma is disrupted, possibly slowing repair via removal of the fibrin scaffold and loss
of early infiltrating cells and cytokines. Fixation of bony surfaces enables primary healing
by creating a low-strain environment. Bone heals directly via cortical remodeling. Areas
not in direct apposition may be filled by woven bone (random orientation) that is
subsequently remodeled to lamellar bone (oriented along the lines of stress). If healing
occurs via endochondral ossification, typically some motion is present at the healing site,
cartilage initially directly bridges the fracture gap to achieve temporary stability, and
intramembranous bone formation works subperiosteally adjacent to the fracture to
convert the cartilage to bone before remodeling.
Secondary bone healing occurs with bone fixation constructs that provide relative
stability (allowing controlled flexibility). Secondary bone healing involves responses in
the periosteum and the surrounding soft tissues. Two types of secondary healing occur:
endochondral and intramembranous. Typically, both types occur concurrently at a
fracture site.
Fracture healing is classically described in three phases. Hematoma formation and
inflammation occur rapidly in the early phases of fracture repair. Macrophages,
neutrophils, and platelets release cytokines, including platelet-derived growth factor
(PDGF), tumor necrosis factor-α, transforming growth factor-ß, and interleukin IL-1, IL-6,
IL-10, and IL-12. Surface osteocytes may survive and are important in synthesizing new
bone. Inflammatory cells migrate to the fracture site, followed by fibroblasts and

chondrocytes. Vasodilation increases local blood flow, and angiogenesis is stimulated,
with capillary ingrowth primarily from the periosteum. Bone morphogenetic proteins
(BMPs) are thought to play an important role in inducing host mesenchymal stem cell
migration and osteoblastic differentiation at the repair site.
During endochondral ossification in the reparative phase, hyaline cartilage created by
chondrocytes provides a framework to bridge fracture fragments and provide early
stabilization. Chondrocytes in cartilage hypertrophy, and the cartilage is subsequently
calcified and replaced by osteoblasts. Calcified cartilage changes to immature woven
bone (soft callus; ie, osteoid). Seams of osteoid surround the core of necrotic bone and
form viable new bone (mineralization, hard callus).
In the remodeling (late) phase, coupled bone resorption and formation occur.
Remodeling is influenced by Wolff’s law. This means that bone remodels along lines of
stress and loading. Remodeling usually is complete within 1 year.
Multiple factors may impair fracture healing. Excessive instability (strain) at the fracture
site or nonapposition of bone may impair healing. Healing also may be impaired by lack
of blood supply because of local vascular anatomy, periosteal stripping from
injury/dissection, or microvascular disease (diabetes mellitus, atherosclerosis). Anti-
inflammatory medications (NSAIDs, steroids), smoking (nicotine and possibly other
effectors), and systemic disease or metabolic bone conditions (eg, osteoporosis, renal
disease, parathyroid dysfunction) may impair healing.

General Principles of Bone Grafting
Several clinical situations may require bone grafting. Spine fusion represents
approximately 50% of bone grafting procedures, and trauma is associated with the next
most frequent use of bone graft. Posterolateral spine fusion is the most difficult spine
fusion environment for healing because of the relatively small area of host bone
(transverse processes), the large gap over which new bone needs to form (2.5 inches),
and the variable motion depending on the extent of spinal fixation. Large segmental
defects, typically associated with high-energy trauma, also are challenging because of
compromised blood supply and the large distance to bridge the new bone. Distal tibial
shaft fractures typically are associated with healing complications because of limited
blood supply and surrounding soft tissue. Delayed or confirmed nonunion may warrant
consideration for bone graft to stimulate healing and revised fixation strategies.
Osteogenic grafts contain live cells that are capable of direct in vivo bone formation.
Osteoprogenitor cells can proliferate and differentiate into osteoblasts and eventually
mature into osteocytes. Mesenchymal stem cells are multipotent and may be induced to
differentiate into bone-forming cells by the local environment. Examples of grafts that
are osteogenic include autologous bone graft, bone marrow aspirate, and possibly some
concentrated mesenchymal stem cell preparations.
Osteoconduction refers to the ability of a graft material to serve as a mechanical three-
dimensional scaffold into which progenitor cells migrate and onto which new bone can
form. The potency of the osteoconductive properties depends on the three-dimensional
configuration (pore size and macro-connecting channels), the building-block material,
and the surface characteristics (macro, micro, and nano). Cancellous bone potentially
has greater surface area, increased porosity for cellular infiltration, and space for
angiogenesis; however, it provides less immediate structural support than cortical bone.

Examples of osteoconductive grafts include autogenous bone graft, acellular allogeneic
cancellous chips, and synthetic bone-void fillers, such as ceramics and bioactive glass.
Multiple proteins are involved in the formation of new bone and incorporation of bone
graft materials. Some of these osteopromotive proteins are capable of enhancing bone
formation already in progress but are not capable of initiating bone formation de novo.
Examples of potentially osteopromotive proteins include PDGF, vascular endothelial
growth factor, and peptides, such as P15.
Osteoinductive graft material is associated with factors that can independently attract
endogenous progenitor cells and induce a bone-forming lineage via cytokines acting as
chemoattractants and differentiation factors. Examples of osteoinductive proteins
include BMP-2, BMP-4, BMP-6, BMP-7, and BMP-9. Usually, osteoinductive materials
must be delivered in combination with an osteoconductive scaffold or other bone graft
material to allow for local retention of the factor and spatially controlled new bone
formation.

Bone graft materials are obtained from various sources and exhibit the bone graft
material properties in various combinations and to various degrees. Different materials
can be combined into a composite graft to deliver multiple graft properties (Resource 5).
Autograft is tissue transferred from one site to another in the same patient and has
classically been the preferred bone graft material. Autograft is the standard by which
other grafting materials are measured. Often, the supply of autograft may be limited,
and procurement may result in short- and long-term donor site morbidity. Autograft is
osteogenic and osteoconductive. Although many classic descriptions of autogenous
bone graft suggest that it has the third graft property, osteoinduction, a more thoughtful
definition would not hold that to be true. Autograft contains natural BMPs; however,
these proteins are not accessible or active because of the mineral phase of autograft,
and implantation of autograft does not result in spontaneous bone formation in a non-
bone location—the Urist definition of osteoinduction.
Autograft may be cortical, cancellous, or corticocancellous; it also may be
nonvascularized or vascularized. Cortical autograft provides structural support; however,
it has higher inorganic mineral density, providing fewer cells for osteogenesis.
Cancellous autograft provides less structural support, higher surface area, greater
cellular components (adjacent to marrow cavities), and less density, yielding greater
osteogenesis and osteoconduction.
Iliac crest bone graft (ICBG) is the most frequently used type of autograft. It has the
potential to provide abundant cancellous and/or cortical graft. Studies have shown
complications associated with ICBG, including chronic pain, hematoma formation,
injuries to the lateral femoral cutaneous or cluneal nerves, infection, fracture, and
scars.1-4 The rate of complications is contested in the literature, with studies conducted
before 2000 demonstrating major complication rates between 0.76% and 25.0% and
minor complication rates, including pain, between 9.4% and 24.0%.5-7 To decrease
complication rates, minimally invasive techniques to harvest bone from the anterior
superior iliac spine and posterior superior iliac spine, generally referred to as the iliac
crest, and from between the inner and outer tables of the iliac crest were developed.
According to clinical studies, the complication rate of ICBG could be reduced by the
development and clinical application of new surgical techniques and instruments.8,

Local autograft (bone from the lamina, spinous process, facet, and osteophytes during
the surgical decompression process) may be obtained from the surgical site. Compared
with ICBG, local bone is considered to be of variable quality, depending on the
proportion of cortical and cancellous bone at the site from which it is obtained, and
quantity, depending on how much host bone is resected. The use of local bone rather
than ICBG can decrease surgical time and prevent unnecessary adverse effects at the
donor site. In the appropriate situation with proper technique, local bone autograft for
spine fusion may be similar to ICBG in terms of fusion rates, pain scores, and functional
outcomes.
Other bone graft sources include the ribs, fibula, and tibial metaphysis. The fibula and
infrequently the ribs are used as vascularized bone graft. Vascularized bone graft may be
used in the management of osteonecrosis of the femoral head, infected nonunion, or
bone defects, we well as for lower limb reconstruction after tumor resection or in
patients with congenital anomaly.
Local autologous bone dust, which is easily collected during drilling with the use of a
high-speed burr, currently is receiving increased attention as an alternative to
autologous bone graft for some less demanding healing situations. Preclinical in vitro
and in vivo studies have validated osteogenesis and osteoconduction of bone dust;
efficacy has been observed in radiographic and clinical outcomes after spine fusion
grafting with the use of local autogenous bone dust.10
Allograft is tissue that is harvested from a cadaver model and/or living donor, processed,
and implanted into another individual of the same species. Because of its availability,
allograft is the bone graft alternative or adjunct most frequently used in patients in the
United States. Allograft can be cortical, cancellous, or corticocancellous. Most allografts
lack viable cells; therefore, allografts do not provide osteogenic properties.
Osteoinductive factors, which may be present in small amounts (not active unless the
bone is demineralized), are reduced by the sterilization necessary to reduce the risk of
disease transmission and avoid host immune responses to the donor graft. Sterilization
techniques also can impair the mechanical properties of the allograft.

Allograft products containing viable cells or those enhanced with viable cells are new to
the market and may offer another grafting option. Tissues selected from a highly
screened donor pool are cryopreserved in a process that maintains cellular viability
(femoral head, vertebral spine, or iliac crest from living donors and/or commercial
allograft products with viable cells). Other similar processes may preserve the proteins in
the allografts and, therefore, maintain more of the osteogenic properties. Several
published clinical studies have detailed the efficacy of allografts described as cellular
bone grafts or allografts with bioavailable growth factors in the field of spine fusion and
joint reconstruction surgery.11,12 This class of allograft remains primarily
osteoconductive; however, it also may have osteogenic and weakly osteoinductive
properties conveyed by the DBM component. Few, if any, studies have validated the
added benefit of the preserved cells above the effect of the associated bone matrix
component of the graft.13
Disease transmission is exceedingly rare with bone allografts and has been most
commonly observed in fresh-frozen (not processed) grafts. Precise incidence data after
2010 are not available (the most recent review was published in 2017 by Fu et al14). The
US FDA has established donor screening and testing; however, few data on rates of
actual disease transmission from allograft to host have been published. Although the
rate of bacterial disease transmission is extremely low, The Centers for Disease Control
and Prevention reported 26 possible cases of bacterial musculoskeletal allograft
infections from 1996 to 2002, including 12 Clostridium species and 11 gram-negative
bacilli.15
The last reports of viral transmission are of hepatitis C in 2002 and human T-cell
lymphocytic virus in 1991. The estimated likelihood of obtaining a graft from an HIV-
positive individual is less than 1 in 1.67 million.16-18 Although no cases have been
documented of prion disease from bone xenografts (bovine derived) or allografts, the
prion infection particle has been isolated in blood products of affected patients, as these
particles are not eliminated by heat or washing processing techniques.
The use of donor material always is associated with a risk of disease transmission or
infection. Regulations and techniques for strict screening, proper procurement, and
processing of donated tissue are continually advancing and enforced by qualified

agencies (such as the American Association of Tissue Banks in the United States). The
extent of osteoconductive properties and mechanical strength depend, in part, on the
method of graft processing and whether the graft is cortical or cancellous bone.
Several types of allograft may be considered. Fresh allograft rarely is used because of the
potential for an immune response and disease transmission and graft-versus-host
disease. Fresh allograft may be processed to remove cells and reduce host immune
reaction. This process has been shown to improve incorporation.
Fresh-frozen washed allograft reduces immunogenicity; frozen allograft requires cold
storage logistics and rewarming (ie, saline) before implantation to avoid brittleness,
which may result in longitudinal fractures. Obtained materials are sterilized via a
chemical washing or radiation method. The chemical washing method is preferred
because of mechanical weakness after the radiation process. Washing also maintains the
osteoconductive properties. The shelf life of fresh-frozen bone is 1 year if it is maintained
at −4°F (−20°C) or 5 years if maintained at −94°F (−70°C).
Collagen is a major component of bone matrix and contributes to mineral deposition,
vascular ingrowth, and growth factor binding, providing a favorable environment for
bone regeneration. It does not provide structural support and may carry immunogenic
potential with allogeneic and xenogeneic use. Collagen functions poorly alone as a bone
graft substitute but can be used as a nonstructural carrier for BMPs, DBM, or other graft
materials.
Freeze-dried washed allograft (prepared by freeze-drying or lyophilization) has
properties similar to those of frozen allograft, with a few exceptions. It is prepared by
freezing the bone, placing it under a vacuum, and obtaining the direct conversion of ice
to vapor. Obtained materials are sterilized via chemical solutions, such as aqueous
solutions of detergents, surfactants, hydrogen peroxides, organic solvents, acids, or
alcohol. Freeze-dried allograft may be stored at room temperature. The shelf life of
freeze-dried bone is indefinite; however, the sterilization of the packaging may expire.
Biomechanical studies have demonstrated compressive and tensile strength similar to
that of frozen allograft but reduced torsional/bending strength compared with fresh or

DBM is allograft processed with a mild acid extraction to remove the mineral content of
bone but keep the collagenous structure (mostly type I, with some types IV and type X)
and non-collagenous proteins. Typically, DBM is combined with carriers, such as
collagen, gelatin, hyaluronic acid, and glycerol, to improve handling characteristics and
deliverability. The antigenic potential and disease transmission related to implantation
are low because of sterilization and other processing.
Theoretically, DBM has osteoinductive activity; however, the level of activity depends on
details of the sterilization process, processing methods, particle size/surface area, and
geometry. Substantial variability exists between products and between production lots
because each production lot is derived from a single patient donor. Ideally, DBM-based
products are osteoconductive and serve as a scaffold for new bone formation; however,
they generally lack structural support. Because of the lack of structural integrity and
limited osteoinductive potential, DBM is frequently mixed with a carrier and used as a
bone graft extender or enhancer in more challenging healing situations rather than as a
stand-alone bone graft substitute. Commonly, DBM is mixed with morcellized autografts,
exogenous peptides, or differentiation factors along with collagen matrix, bone marrow
aspirate, and/or isolated native blood-derived growth factors to stimulate new bone
growth. In previous clinical reports in spine surgery, DBM with autograft, DBM with
growth factors (bone marrow aspiration), and DBM mixed with peptides (recombinant
human BMP-2/acellular collagen sponge) showed potential to substitute for ICBG.21-23
The osteoinductivity and osteoconductivity of DBM vary greatly between brands and
between product formulations from the same manufacturer, making careful validation
of any particular DBM product paramount for justifying its usage.
Bone marrow aspirate is a potential source of mesenchymal stem cells and
osteoprogenitor cells. It may be aspirated percutaneously from the iliac crest, vertebral
body, or other sources. Bone marrow aspirate can be mixed with other bone graft
extenders and ceramics to create a composite graft material. The number of
osteoprogenitor cells varies widely depending on host characteristics, such as age and
sex. The potency of marrow aspirates may be able to be increased via selective

Bioceramics are ionically or covalently bonded calcium phosphate compounds
composed of metallic and nonmetallic elements. The most commonly used bioceramics
are alumina, zirconia, bioactive glass, hydroxyapatite, and TCP. Bioceramics are relatively
inert and demonstrate material properties that are strong in compression but weak in
tension. Bioceramics easily bond with living tissues. They may provide good scaffolds for
the addition of potentially osteogenic cells in skeletal tissue engineering applications.
Several classes of ceramic materials are available. Synthetic hydroxyapatite has the
chemical composition Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2. It typically is used in crystalline form and is slow
to resorb or remodel. For orthopaedic implants, hydroxyapatite usually is coated onto a
metal core or incorporated into polymers as composites. Hydroxyapatite provides a
substrate for bony apposition and ongrowth. The ceramic material ß-TCP has the
chemical composition Ca3(PO4)2. Because of its porous nature and chemical
composition, it is resorbed rapidly. It typically is developed for orthopaedic implants as a
porous biphasic calcium phosphate scaffold with 60% hydroxyapatite and 40% ß-TCP. An
osteoconductive effect or scaffold is provided, which varies based on the pore size of the
synthesized material. Larger pore sizes (>50 μm) provide more space for the migration
and ingrowth of osteogenic cells and vascular supply.
Other materials, such as bioactive glass, contain silicone salt combinations. Bioactive
glass has been used for various clinical applications since its creation in 1969. Many
types of bioactive glass (eg, 45S5, S53P4) and glass-based products are used in
periodontal repair and orthopaedic applications. These materials typically interact with
body fluids and, through a salt exchange, form an amorphous layer of hydroxyapatite
(nanocrystalline hydroxyapatite). Glass-based materials provide the scaffold for bony
apposition, forming a strong bond with natural bone. The mechanism for the formation
of the nanocrystalline hydroxyapatite layer is well understood and characterized;
however, the biologic interactions between the nanocrystalline hydroxyapatite and the
host bone interface are under intense investigation given potential recruitment of stem

Bioceramics alone possess no osteogenic or osteoinductive properties, and they have
variable early and ongoing structural support secondary to resorption. Bioceramics
based on TCP and/or hydroxyapatite may be used in combination with biologic
osteoinductive or osteogenic supplements, such as autograft, BMP, bioactive glass, bone
marrow aspirate, growth factors, or mesenchymal stem cell derivatives. Studies
demonstrate improved function and reduced pain to the same extent as that after the
use of ICBG; however, bioceramics have been associated with suboptimal radiographic
fusion rates (density on radiographs) in the lumbar spine compared with ICBG.25 The
most successful use of bioceramics as a graft substitute/extender has been in the fusion
of the relatively rigid thoracic spine in adolescent patients with idiopathic scoliosis. These
materials have been far less effective in adult patients undergoing fusion for the
management of lumbar degeneration.

Peptide-Based Materials
The peptide P15 is a bioactive synthetic multidomain peptide from type I collagen
(Resource 6). It has been reported to enhance cell adhesion, osteoblastic gene
expression, and mineralization on bovine-derived acellular hydroxyapatite matrix in vitro
and accelerates early bone formation in porcine and rat cranial defects.26,27 It is
delivered in an anorganic bone matrix composed of calcium phosphate, which provides
osteoconductive properties that support cell invasion and migration. In the clinical field,
P15 peptide-coated anorganic bone matrix has been used in the management of human
periodontal bony defects, resulting in better clinical outcomes than open flap
débridement alone, and it also has been used in a pilot clinical study for the
SEND FEEDBACK

management of long bone defects.28,29 In a prospective, randomized, single-blinded trial
of single-level anterior cervical diskectomy and fusion with the use of P15 in an allograft
spacer versus local autologous bone graft in an allograft spacer, fusion rates of 89.0%
versus 85.8% were reported, respectively, at 1-year follow-up, with equivalent clinical
outcomes and complications.30 The challenge with this study design is the lack of an
empty allograft spacer control; therefore the study does not confirm the independent
effect of P15.
Although PDGF is a naturally occurring molecule released by several cell types, it was
first identified and isolated from platelets. The growth factor is released from the a-
granules of platelets as part of the clotting and inflammatory process. During bone
healing, the release of PDGF results in paracrine signaling for the recruitment and
mitogenesis of mesenchymal stem cells, fibroblasts, vascular smooth muscle cells, and
osteoblasts, which are critical to the early phases of new bone formation. Among the
PDGF family of growth factors is PDGF-BB, the universal isoform that can bind to all
known receptor isotypes. A commercially available composite of recombinant human
PDGF-BB with ß-TCP granules received FDA premarket approval in 2015 for clinical use
as an alternative to autograft in patients undergoing ankle/hindfoot arthrodesis.
Although it has yet to be investigated thoroughly in patients undergoing spinal
arthrodesis, results for bony fusion are promising.31 In a 36-week prospective,
multicenter pilot trial, 90% of patients treated with this product for ankle and/or
hindfoot fusion were considered a clinical success, and 88% exhibited radiographic
union. Fusion rates were deemed comparable with the results of autogenous bone graft
in historical control patients.32-34

Bone Morphogenetic Proteins
The BMP family contains at least 20 unique proteins (differentiation factors/peptides)
that have been identified and are members of the transforming growth factor-ß
superfamily. BMPs play a key role in normal embryonic development. Many but not all
BMPs are osteoinductive; some are unrelated to bone formation or have alternative
functions (BMP-1 and BMP-3).
Two recombinant human BMPs underwent clinical trials for FDA approval. Recombinant
human BMP-2 received FDA approval in 2002 for use in anterior lumbar interbody
fusion. Recombinant human BMP-7 did not receive full FDA approval but was allowed to
be used under humanitarian device exemption. These recombinant human BMPs are
highly water soluble; therefore, a carrier or delivery material is used to bind the BMP
solution and retain it at the implantation site. Without efficient binding to the carrier or
matrix substance (suboptimal binding), recombinant human BMPs in solution will rapidly
diffuse from a prepared surgical site, wound bed, or fracture site, or be inadvertently
removed by irrigation.
The FDA approved recombinant human BMP-2 for anterior lumbar interbody fusion in
patients with degenerative disk disease and grade I spondylolisthesis (2002), for the
management of tibial nonunion as an alternative to autograft (2004), and for oral
maxillofacial reconstruction (2007). During the past decade, recombinant human BMP-2
has been commonly used off-label (ie, physician-directed use) in posterior lumbar
interbody fusion, transforaminal interbody fusion, and posterolateral lumbar fusion. The
FDA approved recombinant human BMP-7 for use in patients with recalcitrant long bone
nonunion (2001) and expanded the authorization to posterolateral lumbar fusion under
a humanitarian device exemption (2004); however, it is not currently marketed in the
United States. The clinical formulation of recombinant human BMP-7 (dose and carrier)
was not optimized for use in primates and likely was underdosed, resulting in
inconsistent bone induction.
In addition, recombinant human BMP-2 has been used off-label in pediatric spine fusion.
The safety of recombinant human BMP-2 in children has not been established despite

Safety always is a consideration in the use of recombinant human BMP in elective spine
surgery and in off-label use according to surgical technique and local anatomy. Well-
known complications associated with the use of recombinant human BMPs in cervical
and lumbar spine fusion include extradiscal, ectopic, or heterotrophic bone formation;
resorption/osteolysis; graft subsidence and cage migration; wound complications
(including hematoma and seroma); dysphagia; radiculitis; antibody formation; toxicity;
and carcinogenesis. Many of the local adverse effects reported soon after initial approval
resulted from relative overdosing of recombinant human BMP-2 in some off-label uses.
According to a recent large-pool cohort analysis (460,773 patients from 2005 to 2010),
the overall risk of a postoperative complication after lumbar spine fusion surgery
(anterior or posterior techniques) was not increased regardless of recombinant human
BMP-2 use.35 In a recent large cohort study (215,047 patients from 2005 to 2011),
surgical wound complications, such as epidural hematoma, wound dehiscence,
postoperative fever, and hemorrhage, were higher in patients treated with recombinant
human BMP-2; however, other complications, such as abnormal inflammatory reaction
(eg, dysphagia or hoarseness [cervical]), neurologic complications, and medical
problems, were similar in patients treated with recombinant human BMP-2 and patients
not treated with recombinant human BMP-2.36,37
The possible carcinogenicity of recombinant human BMP is a subject of debate. A study
using FDA clinical trial data for recombinant human BMP-2 use in posterolateral fusion
showed an association between high-dose recombinant human BMP-2 and higher
malignancy rates. The authors suggested that a 40-mg dose of recombinant human
BMP-2 with compression-resistant matrix during posterolateral lumbar spinal
arthrodesis was associated with an increased rate of new malignancies in patients
treated with BMP and compression-resistant matrix (12 of 155 patients; 7.7%), compared
with patients treated with ICBG (5 of 137 patients; 3.6%). However, this report was from
a relatively small sample, the study did not verify homogeneity between patients treated

Other Modalities to Enhance Bone Healing
Bone tissue has bioelectric potential. Bioelectric potential is electronegative in areas of
growth or healing. The area returns to neutral or electropositive as healing progresses.
Bioelectric potential is electronegative in areas of compression and electropositive in
areas of tension. Trials have shown substantial variability in outcomes, with overall
efficacy unclear.44 Advantages have been seen in single studies for some fracture

types.45 Because of the low morbidity associated with the treatment, the clinical use of
electromagnetic stimulation is common despite its unclear efficacy.
Types of electromagnetic stimulation include pulsed electromagnetic field, in which
alternating current is delivered through an external coil, used intermittently during the
treatment period; capacitively coupled electrical stimulation, in which current is
delivered between two plates that form a magnetic field over the site of healing; and
direct current electrical stimulation, which is delivered through implanted electrodes. 
Low-intensity ultrasonography may affect bone healing; however, clinical use is not in
widespread. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasonography (LIPUS) may result in nanomotion,
which causes a mechanical signal that is converted to a biochemical signal inside the
cells, stimulating signal transduction, blood flow, and angiogenesis and promoting
protein synthesis, calcium uptake, and osteogenic gene expression at the fracture site.
The US FDA and the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence approved LIPUS
for the management of fresh fractures (1994) and for the management of delayed
unions and nonunions (2000). The UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
presented a statement supporting the use of LIPUS to reduce fracture healing time and
to provide clinical benefit, particularly in circumstances of delayed healing and
nonunion. Recently, LIPUS also was used for early bone healing for distraction
osteogenesis.46,47
A substantial positive effect of LIPUS in the management of fresh fractures was identified
in prospective, randomized, multicenter, double-blind level I clinical studies investigating
LIPUS in patients undergoing nonsurgical management of tibial and distal radius
fractures (38% acceleration of fracture repair) in 1994.48,49 For nonunion (ie, fractures
that had not healed after 9 months), a greater than85% healing rate was reported after
daily LIPUS for 3 months;50 however, the clinical effects of LIPUS are a subject of debate.
Recent large-pool database studies provide evidence with moderate to high certainty to
support a strong recommendation against the use of LIPUS for bone healing at fracture
sites and for osteotomy site healing during distraction osteogenesis procedures.51-53
